# Pānīyajātaka (Ja 459)

**ID:** Ja 459
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (Pali):** Pānīyajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Stolen Drink

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Pānīyajātaka* (Ja 459) is a narrative in the Pali *Jātaka* collection concerned with the subduing of evil passions and the moral power of remorse [SuttaCentral; Granoff and Shinohara 2012]. In the traditional frame story recorded in the commentary, the Buddha delivers the discourse while dwelling at Jetavana to five hundred ordained lay-companions from Sāvatthī who were disturbed by sensual thoughts (*kāmavitakka*) in the middle of the night; he admonishes them that no defilement is insignificant and that even the slightest taint must be restrained by the wise [Fausböll 1887]. The core narrative illustrates how individuals attained the status of *paccekabuddha* through conscience and renunciation triggered by small moral failings [Fausböll 1887; Granoff and Shinohara 2012]. It opens with two farmers working their fields with separate water pots; one secretly drinks from his companion's pot to conserve his own supply, but is immediately seized by horror and remorse at his deed, realizing that unchecked thirst would cause him to fall into ruin, which prompts him to abandon worldly life so as never to commit evil again [Granoff and Shinohara 2012]. The tale also mentions a band of robbers designated as "The Senders" or "Despatchers" [Gjellerup 1999]. At the story's conclusion, the Buddha identifies the previous births, noting that the *paccekabuddha*s have entered final extinguishment, the queen was Rāhulamātā, and the king was the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1887].

SuttaCentral records no curated external parallels for the text [SuttaCentral]. Computational analysis via DharmaNexus confirms internal text reuse between the canonical verses and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (fourth volume), identifying seventeen matching segments (with the longest matching sequence spanning §0.4–4.4 against commentary sections §1088_5–1102 at 0.91 similarity), while recording no cross-language matches in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan corpora meeting the threshold score [DharmaNexus].
